readerTitle: Why the baker's 20 notes beat 500 emails
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (동네 베이커리의 카페 납품 영업, 병원 예약 소프트웨어 창업자) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 콜드 아웃리치는 나를 알리는 일이 아니라, 상대가 이미 겪는 문제를 상대의 말로 먼저 짚어 주고 작은 다음 걸음을 제안하는 일이다.
misconception: 콜드 아웃리치는 숫자 게임이다. 많이 보낼수록 더 많이 팔린다.

sources.text: 설명용 가상 사례. 일반적인 B2B·지역 영업 실무 원칙에 기반

factChecks.note: 응답 수(베이커리 20통 중 6곳 회신, 소프트웨어 500통 중 3건 회신)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 평균 응답률로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 라벨이 붙어 있는지 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 스팸·광고성 연락 규제 언급은 일반적인 주의 문구입니다. 특정 국가 법률(예: 미국 CAN-SPAM, EU GDPR, 한국 정보통신망법)의 내용을 설명하지 않도록 유지하세요.
'메시지당 10분이면 하루 약 20통' 계산: 20 × 10분 = 200분(약 3시간 20분). 다른 업무와 병행하는 창업자 기준으로 현실적인 수치인지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Why the baker's 20 notes beat 500 emails
body: In the same week, two founders reach out to strangers. A baker writes to 20 local cafés. A software founder emails 500 clinics.
The baker sends far fewer messages and gets more replies. The difference isn't luck or charm. It's what each message is about.

image.label: A handwritten note next to a huge stack of identical emails
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에는 크루아상 상자 위에 손글씨 쪽지 한 장, 오른쪽에는 똑같은 이메일 봉투가 산처럼 쌓여 있음. 왼쪽 쪽지에만 작은 답장 말풍선이 여러 개 붙어 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your first message to a café owner
body: Mina runs a small bakery. She wants to sell croissants wholesale to cafés nearby. She has never met these owners.
Which first message is most likely to get a reply?

options.text: "Hi, I'm Mina. My bakery uses French butter and won a local award. Can we set up a 30-minute meeting?"
options.feedback: It's polite and true, but it's all about Mina, and it asks a busy stranger for half an hour. Easy to ignore.

options.text: "Your pastry case looks empty by 11 on weekdays. I bake at 5 and can deliver by 7. Can I drop off a free box Thursday for your staff?"
options.feedback: It names something she actually saw and asks for almost nothing. It costs her research time, but it gives the owner a reason to answer.

options.text: A well-designed price list and brochure, emailed to 100 cafés
options.feedback: It reaches more people and looks professional. But it answers "what do you sell?" before anyone asked, so most owners won't open it.

cards.title: Two founders, two approaches.
body: Mina spent about ten minutes on each café. She stopped by at lunch, read their reviews and wrote three sentences about something she had seen herself.
Daniel, the software founder, wrote one email: "Our AI platform transforms clinic scheduling. Can we book a 30-minute demo?" He sent it 500 times.
Mina heard back from 6 cafés. Daniel got 3 replies. Two asked to be removed from his list.

cards.title: Cold outreach
body: **Cold outreach** means contacting people who don't know you yet, to start a conversation that could become a sale. It can be an email, a call, a walk-in or a direct message.
A stranger owes you nothing, so their default is to ignore you. A cold message has one job: give them a reason to reply within seconds. That reason is almost never you. **It's them.**

cards.title: Anatomy of a message that gets a reply
body: Mina's note to one café had four short parts.

breakdown.label: Why you
breakdown.detail: "Your pastry case looks empty by 11 on weekdays."

breakdown.label: Why it matters
breakdown.detail: "That's when office workers come in for a snack."

breakdown.label: Why me
breakdown.detail: "I bake at 5 and can deliver by 7."

breakdown.label: A small ask
breakdown.detail: "Can I drop off a free box Thursday?"

cards.callout: Notice what's missing: her life story, her awards and a request for a meeting.
cards.softwareNote: The same four parts work in software: name a problem you saw ("your booking page needs a phone call to reschedule"), why it matters, what you do about it, and a tiny next step.

cards.title: Replies are also information.
body: A specific message works because it proves you did your homework and makes saying yes cheap. That holds anywhere: a cleaning company writing to property managers, or a manager asking another team for help.
Early on, replies are data too. If ten specific notes about the same problem get silence, the problem may not hurt enough. That is worth learning before you build or bake more.

cards.title: Specific doesn't scale, and that's fine.
body: Research takes time. At ten minutes a message, you might send about 20 a day alongside other work. At this stage you need real conversations, not reach.
Fake personalization backfires. Dropping a first name into a template isn't specific, and people can tell.
Rules on unsolicited emails and calls differ by country. Check what applies to you before sending at volume.

cards.title: Now it's a software founder.
body: Daniel's app cuts missed appointments at small dental clinics. After his 500 emails flopped, he has one week to try again.

options.text: Buy a list of 2,000 clinic emails and send an automated five-step sequence
options.feedback: More volume of a message nobody wanted. He gains reach but risks spam complaints and learns almost nothing about why clinics stay silent.

options.text: Pick 25 clinics, read their reviews for complaints about waits or rescheduling, and send each a three-sentence note offering a free look at their no-show pattern
options.feedback: Fewer messages, but each one names a problem the clinic already has and asks for something small. Replies, or silence, will also tell him if the problem is real.

options.text: Keep the same email but insert each clinic's name and city
options.feedback: Cheap to do and slightly warmer. But the message is still about his platform, not about anything he noticed at their clinic.

cards.softwareNote: Tools make it easy to send thousands of emails. That makes a message clearly written for one reader stand out even more.

cards.title: Start with their situation. Ask for something small.
body: A cold message earns a reply when it shows you noticed something real about the reader and makes the next step easy.
**Try it today:** pick five possible customers. For each, write one sentence about something specific you noticed about their business. If you can't, you're not ready to message them yet.
